title_en: Zhongji General Import and Export Company v. Tianjin Port Second Harbor Co., Ltd. — dispute over port operation contract
keywords_en: Civil; Dispute over port operation contract; First instance; Basic People's Court; Tianjin City; Legal person; Rules for Carriage of Goods by Water; Determination of force majeure; Litigation subject qualification of actual operation client; Custody liability of port operator; Dismissal of claims; Port operation contract; Cargo damage caused by storm surge; Cargo arrival at port; Contract dispute; Dispute over port operation contract of a limited company
full_text_en:
Zhongji General Import and Export Company v. Tianjin Port Second Stevedoring Co., Ltd. — dispute over port operation contract

Plaintiff: Zhongji General Import and Export Company.

Legal Representative: Yuan Yiping, General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Wang Shengran, Attorney at Beijing Zhongfu Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Han Guohua, Attorney at Tianjin Jinhua Law Firm.

Defendant: Tianjin Port Authority Second Stevedoring Co., Ltd.

Legal Representative: Liu Baoen, General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Ma Guilan, Staff Member of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Fang Guoqing, Attorney at Yuanhai Law Firm.

The plaintiff, Zhongji General Import and Export Company (hereinafter referred to as Zhongji Company), filed a lawsuit with the Tianjin Maritime Court against the defendant, Tianjin Port Authority Second Stevedoring Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Stevedoring Company), due to a dispute over a port operation contract.

The plaintiff alleged: On August 19, 1997, the plaintiff, in accordance with the defendant's notice, transported the plaintiff's export goods to the defendant's dock, preparing to load them onto the vessel on August 20, 1997, as agreed in the port operation contract. The defendant issued a receipt confirming receipt of all the plaintiff's goods. On August 20, Typhoon No. 9711 made landfall. Despite receiving prior forecasts, the defendant failed to take any preventive measures for the plaintiff's goods, resulting in the goods being soaked by sea tide and rendered unusable, causing losses to the plaintiff amounting to RMB 5,622,840. Subsequently, the defendant refused to compensate on the grounds that "the loss was caused by force majeure." The plaintiff argued that, given the advanced state of technology today, adverse weather conditions that have been forecast no longer constitute unforeseeable force majeure, and the defendant cannot use this to evade liability. The plaintiff requested a court ruling ordering the defendant to bear liability for compensation.

The defendant argued: (1) The fact that the plaintiff's goods were damaged exists, but these goods were handled by the defendant under a port operation contract signed with a third party, Tianjin Development Zone Xinxing Trading Company (hereinafter referred to as Xinxing Company). There is no contractual relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant. Even if the defendant was at fault in this port operation contract, it should be the other party, Xinxing Company, that sues the defendant; no other person has the right to sue the defendant. (2) The defendant could only take emergency measures based on the forecast issued by the National Marine Environmental Forecasting Center, and in fact, preventive measures were taken. However, because the incoming tide exceeded the forecast level and was accompanied by rain, despite the defendant's best efforts, it was impossible to avoid the damage to these goods. Such damage was truly caused by force majeure—unforeseeable, unavoidable, and insurmountable—for which the defendant should not bear liability for compensation according to law.

The Tianjin Maritime Court found the following facts upon trial:

The plaintiff, Zhongji Company, in order to export sodium tripolyphosphate and acetylene black, entered into a freight forwarding agency contract with the third party, Xinxing Company, agreeing to entrust Xinxing Company to, in Xinxing Company's name, declare the cargo consolidation plan to the defendant, Stevedoring Company, handle cargo delivery, and pay port charges, etc. After Xinxing Company declared the cargo consolidation plan to Stevedoring Company, Stevedoring Company notified Xinxing Company to consolidate cargo on August 18, 1997. On that day, Xinxing Company notified Zhongji Company to consolidate 2,498 tons of sodium tripolyphosphate, and on the morning of the next day, another 94 tons of sodium tripolyphosphate and 150 tons of acetylene black were consolidated. These goods were placed by Stevedoring Company at its storage yards No. 2, No. 3, and No. 7, with elevations of 5.1 meters to 5.3 meters, awaiting loading. At 15:54 on August 20, due to the impact of Typhoon No. 9711, 1,074 tons of sodium tripolyphosphate and 43.3 tons of acetylene black were damaged by seawater immersion. At 16:30, Stevedoring Company notified Xinxing Company of the goods being soaked by seawater and issued a cargo damage certificate on August 22.

Regarding Typhoon No. 9711, the National Marine Environmental Forecasting Center issued its first forecast at 08:00 on August 19, 1997, predicting that due to the influence of Typhoon No. 9711, the tide level would reach 5.10 meters at 16:00 on August 19, while the actual tide level at 16:30 on August 19 was 4.82 meters. At 16:00 on August 19, the Forecasting Center issued its second forecast, predicting that at 04:00 on August 20, the tide level would reach 5.20 meters, while the actual tide level at 04:04 on August 20 was 4.96 meters. At 08:00 on August 20, the Forecasting Center issued its third forecast, predicting that at 16:50 on August 20, the tide level would reach 5.30 meters, while the actual tide level at 15:54 on August 20 was 5.59 meters. In addition, according to the meteorological technical consultation report from the Tianjin Tanggu District Meteorological Bureau, during the passage of Typhoon No. 9711, there was rain at Tianjin Tanggu New Port from 01:28 to 01:35 and from 04:17 to 18:06 on August 20, accompanied by gusts of wind of force 8 or above.

After receiving the warning about Typhoon No. 9711 at approximately 10:00 on August 19, 1997, the defendant, Stevedoring Company, took the following measures regarding the 39,612.078 tons of goods in storage: transported over 1,500 tons by train for evacuation, moved over 1,200 tons, with the goods including machinery, rolled steel, barley, fishmeal, etc. Before the arrival of the sea tide, Stevedoring Company took no measures regarding the goods belonging to the plaintiff, Zhongji Company. Apart from the damage to Zhongji Company's goods, goods of others stored in Stevedoring Company's warehouses and yards were also soaked by seawater to varying degrees.

After the damage to the plaintiff, Zhongji Company's goods, Zhongji Company requested the manufacturer of sodium tripolyphosphate to conduct technical tests, which proved that the sodium tripolyphosphate soaked by seawater could no longer be used normally. Regarding the damaged acetylene black, Zhongji Company did not produce an inspection report.

The above facts are confirmed by the agency agreement between the plaintiff, Zhongji Company, and the third party, Xinxing Company; the port operation contract between Xinxing Company and the defendant, Stevedoring Company; the cargo damage certificate issued by Stevedoring Company; the technical test certificate from the manufacturer of sodium tripolyphosphate; the forecast records of the National Marine Environmental Forecasting Center regarding Typhoon No. 9711 storm surge; the work orders for moving and evacuating goods by Stevedoring Company; the meteorological technical consultation report from the Tianjin Tanggu District Meteorological Bureau; and the statements of the parties.

The Tianjin Maritime Court held:

Article 4, Item 2 of the "Rules for Waterway Cargo Transportation" promulgated by the Ministry of Communications provides: "A port operation contract refers to a contract under which the port operator collects port charges and is responsible for loading, unloading, storing, lightering, and other operations for the transport goods entrusted by the operation client." The goods damaged in this case were stored in the port yard based on a port operation contract; therefore, the parties should be the defendant, Stevedoring Company, as the port operator, and the operation client. Article 4, Item 7 of the "Rules for Waterway Cargo Transportation" provides: "Operation client refers to a person who personally or through another person, in his own name or through another person on his behalf, enters into an operation contract with the port operator." The plaintiff, Zhongji Company, and the third party, Xinxing Company, entered into an agency agreement to better accomplish port operations such as cargo consolidation. Although the agent, Xinxing Company, declared the cargo consolidation plan to Stevedoring Company and handled cargo delivery in its own name, the owner of the damaged goods in this case is Zhongji Company, and Xinxing Company has no interest in the cargo damage. Therefore, although Zhongji Company did not directly enter into a port operation contract with Stevedoring Company, it was indeed the actual operation client who entered into the port operation contract with Stevedoring Company under the name of Xinxing Company, and thus is the proper plaintiff in this case.

The goods belonging to the plaintiff, Zhongji Company, suffered damage due to the onslaught of Typhoon No. 9711 while in the custody of the defendant, Stevedoring Company. The facts are clear, and both parties have no dispute. Under normal circumstances, Stevedoring Company has a duty to properly safeguard goods transported to its yard awaiting loading, which is a legal obligation of the port operator.

Before the arrival of Typhoon No. 9711, the National Marine Environmental Forecasting Center issued forecasts, and the first two forecast tide levels were higher than the actual tide levels. Had the situation continued in this manner, the argument that "the storm surge was unforeseeable" could not be sustained. The issue is that when Typhoon No. 9711 reached Tianjin Tanggu New Port, it coincided with the astronomical spring tide period, causing tide levels to rise 160-193 cm above normal annual levels. Additionally, the wind direction was northeast, with wind speeds of 14-15 m/s (force 7), resulting in wave heights of 1 meter inside the harbor basin and 2 meters outside, both exceeding the safety warning level. On the afternoon of August 20, when Zhongji Company's goods were soaked by seawater, the National Marine Environmental Forecasting Center predicted a tide level of 5.30 meters at 16:50, but the actual tide level at 15:54 had already reached 5.59 meters, exceeding the forecast by 29 cm. It was the combination of the storm surge, astronomical spring tide, and sea waves that exacerbated the tidal disaster, causing seawater to surge onto the dock and soak Zhongji Company's goods. Such a disaster was not foreseen even by the professional National Marine Environmental Forecasting Center, let alone by Stevedoring Company.

Second, under the imminent threat of Typhoon No. 9711, the defendant, Stevedoring Company, took appropriate protective measures for all goods stored in its yard. The "appropriate protective measures" referred to here are those applicable to all goods for which Stevedoring Company was obligated to provide proper care. After receiving the storm forecast, Stevedoring Company, based on its own resources, over the period of more than one day from August 19 to August 20, in addition to continuing normal loading operations, took temporary preventive measures, moving over 1,200 tons of goods and evacuating over 1,500 tons by railway, effectively reducing overall cargo losses. Considering that the storage yard for Zhongji Company's goods had a relatively higher elevation compared to other goods, and that the forecasted higher tide level had not yet arrived, Stevedoring Company did not take anti-tide measures for Zhongji Company's goods. As a result, when an unforeseeable high tide later occurred, Zhongji Company's goods were soaked by seawater. This was an unavoidable natural disaster. The fact that Zhongji Company's goods, among the overall goods in Stevedoring Company's yard, suffered damage does not mean that Stevedoring Company abandoned concern for the safety of the goods. Stevedoring Company did its utmost to ensure the safety of the goods in its custody. The damage to Zhongji Company's goods indeed occurred under circumstances that Stevedoring Company could not resist, and Stevedoring Company had no subjective fault regarding this loss.

Article 73, Paragraph 1, Item 9 of the "Rules for Waterway Cargo Transportation" provides: "During the port operator's period of responsibility, if goods are contaminated, damaged, or suffer other losses not caused by the port operator, and such losses are caused by force majeure, the port operator shall not be liable for compensation." Stevedoring Company's defense that it should not bear liability for the cargo damage in this case is well-founded.

In conclusion, the Tianjin Maritime Court ruled:

The plaintiff's claim is rejected.

The litigation costs of this case, RMB 38,124, shall be borne by the plaintiff, Zhongji Company.

Zhongji Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Tianjin High People's Court, arguing: Typhoon No. 9711 had been forecast, and the appellee, Stevedoring Company, should have foreseen it. Under such circumstances, Stevedoring Company's failure to take appropriate preventive measures for the appellant's goods, resulting in damage, does not satisfy the legal conditions for force majeure. Second, after receiving the warning, Stevedoring Company, knowing that the forecast tide level far exceeded the safety warning level and that the forecast tide level already exceeded the elevation of the dock where the appellant's goods were stored (meaning seawater would definitely come ashore), took no measures to fulfill its legal obligation to protect the goods from damage. Stevedoring Company was subjectively at fault for this cargo damage and should bear fault liability. The appellant requested that the second-instance court set aside the first-instance judgment, remand the case for retrial, or amend the judgment according to law.

Stevedoring Company argued: After receiving the storm forecast at approximately 10:00 on August 19, 1997, the appellee immediately held an emergency meeting, notified the operation clients to stop cargo consolidation, urgently mobilized all available port machinery for rush loading, and moved goods stored at lower elevations to warehouses with higher elevations. The appellant's goods were stored in a yard with an elevation of 5.1-5.3 meters, and with the addition of pallets, the elevation reached approximately 5.4-5.6 meters, higher than other goods stored in yards with an elevation of 4.7 meters. Given the imminent storm surge, the appellee should first consider moving goods stored in yards with an elevation of 4.7 meters. Due to the short time, combined with rainfall and force 7-8 winds at the time, and the fact that many goods (including Zhongji Company's goods) were susceptible to rain and could not be handled, forcibly moving them at that time might have caused even greater losses. The appellant was one of the appellee's clients, and the appellee had no bias against the appellant's goods. If the appellee had prioritized moving the appellant's goods while ignoring goods stored at lower elevations, this would not have been in line with professional practices for port operators and would also have been unfair to other cargo owners. The loss of the appellant's goods was indeed caused by force majeure, and the appellee was not at fault for this loss. The first-instance judgment was correct and should be affirmed.

After trial, the Tianjin High People's Court held: "Force majeure" as referred to in law means objective circumstances that are unforeseeable, unavoidable, and insurmountable. After the arrival of Typhoon No. 9711, although the National Marine Environmental Forecasting Center issued forecasts, under the current state of science and technology, from the time the forecast was issued to the time the appellant's goods were damaged, the appellee, Stevedoring Company, was unable to ensure the safety of all goods in its custody. Therefore, the damage to Zhongji Company's goods was still caused by unavoidable force majeure. Zhongji Company's appeal argument that because Typhoon No. 9711 had been forecast, it was not unforeseeable and therefore the loss was not caused by force majeure, lacks legal basis and is not supported. As a port operator, after receiving the forecast of Typhoon No. 9711 storm surge, Stevedoring Company mobilized a large number of personnel and mechanical equipment to accelerate loading and moving and evacuating goods, fulfilling its duties as a port operator. Due to factors such as rainfall accompanied by strong winds, time constraints, mechanical equipment, and the nature of the goods, it was reasonable for Stevedoring Company not to move certain goods, including Zhongji Company's goods, that were susceptible to rain or stored at higher elevations. Therefore, Stevedoring Company is not liable for the damage to Zhongji Company's goods. The appellee's arguments are accepted. The first-instance judgment had clear findings of fact and correct application of law, and should be affirmed. Accordingly, the Tianjin High People's Court, in accordance with Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, on February 13, 2000, ruled:

The appeal is dismissed, and the original judgment is affirmed.

The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 38,124 shall be borne by the appellant, Zhongji Company.
